strengths: Clear and relevant problem: model provenance for open-source LLMs is practically important, and the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing backdoor-based fingerprints lack reliability/robustness guarantees while OSM watermarks harm quality and are removed by finetuning.

The core idea (restrict watermarking to a provider-chosen target domain) is simple but well-motivated, and directly inherits the desirable statistical properties of watermarks (controlled Type-1 error, monotonicity of detection power with #queries) into the fingerprinting setting.

The method is practical and well-instantiated: KGW logit-distillation plus a one-sided total-variation regularization loss (Eq. 4) that preserves utility outside the target domain, with clean algorithmic presentation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation against the desiderata: reliability (Fig. 2), harmlessness (PPL, GPT-4 judge, benchmarks in Tables 1-2), persistence under in/out-of-domain finetuning (Table 3, Figs. 3, 6), robustness to system prompts and greedy sampling (Figs. 4, 7, 8), and qualitative stealthiness (Fig. 5).

Direct head-to-head comparisons with prior backdoor-based fingerprints (instructional fingerprints, scalable fingerprints) in the appendix, showing those methods lose persistence and robustness under non-adversarial system prompts and finetuning—strengthening the empirical claims.

Useful ablations and extensions: KGW hyperparameter ablation (App. B), multiple coexisting keys (App. C.2), domain-leakage analysis (App. C.3, honestly presented as a limitation), watermark-token triggers, and a harmful-content domain experiment.
Good clarity overall: desiderata are explicitly defined (Sec. 3), threat model is stated, and limitations are discussed candidly (Sec. 6, App. C.3).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially watermark logit-distillation from Gu et al. [17] combined with a domain-restricted dataset and a one-sided TV regularization term. The contribution is the reframing/insight rather than a new mechanism, and no theoretical analysis of the regularization or persistence is provided.

Narrow evaluation scope: only two models (1B and 7B) and only the KGW watermark are tested; robustness of the finding to other watermark schemes (e.g., distortion-free or stronger univariate schemes) or larger models is unknown.

Statistical claims are under-validated: Type-1 error control is asserted from the asymptotic normality of the KGW Z-test, but the null distribution is only verified for unwatermarked base models (p≈0.5) with limited repetitions; the validity of extreme p-values (<1e-5) after finetuning is not empirically checked, so the claimed formal guarantees at the stated thresholds are somewhat stronger than the evidence.

The stealthiness argument is largely qualitative (a single example in Fig. 5). Notably, in-domain watermarking substantially degrades in-domain quality (e.g., French Q&A: GPT-judge 6.00→3.33, PPL 4.38→11.1 for Llama3.2-1B in Table 1), which an adversary could plausibly detect—creating tension with the stealthiness claim that is not analyzed.

Persistence under the adversarial case (finetuning on the target domain) degrades significantly, and for Math on Qwen the fingerprint is not recoverable at all; the 'choose a high-entropy domain' mitigation shifts the burden to the provider without analysis of how providers should trade off domain relevance vs. watermark capacity.

Comparison setup against baselines could be fairer: the paper's own method is evaluated with tuned regularization, while baseline implementations (e.g., the scalable fingerprint adaptation with weight decay instead of model merging) involve substitutions that may handicap the originals.
Some key hyperparameters (e.g., the regularization weight λ in Algorithm 2) are not ablated in the main experiments, limiting reproducibility of the quality/power trade-off.
Missing comparison to other black-box fingerprinting works (e.g., LLMMap) and to adaptive adversaries who might specifically query or sanitize the chosen target domain.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and practically important problem: black-box model provenance/ownership detection for open-source LLMs shared under restrictive licenses, a setting where existing weight-access or backdoor-based fingerprints fall short.

The framing is clear and well organized: the paper defines a concrete threat model and a set of desiderata (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness), and systematically evaluates against each.

The proposed method is technically plausible and simple: restricting watermark logit-distillation (KGW, following Gu et al.) to a target domain with a one-sided total-variation regularization loss (Eq. 4) that constrains positive deviations from the teacher outside the domain.

The evaluation covers several axes: reliability across query counts, persistence under multiple finetuning datasets and regimes, robustness to system prompts and greedy sampling, plus direct comparisons with two backdoor-based fingerprinting baselines (instructional and scalable fingerprints) in the appendix.

Useful supporting analyses: hyperparameter ablations over KGW parameters (App. B), watermark-token experiments, multi-key experiments, domain-leakage analysis, and license/reproducibility documentation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is essentially applying an existing OSM watermark distillation technique (Gu et al. [17]) to a restricted domain with a simple regularization term. The key idea (watermark only a subdomain instead of all outputs) is an obvious relaxation, and no new watermarking, training, or detection machinery is introduced. The 'monotonicity' property and statistical FPR guarantees are inherited from prior watermarking work rather than contributed.

The 'harmlessness' claim is overstated. Table 1 shows substantial quality degradation inside the target domain (e.g., French PPL 4.38 -> 11.1 and GPT-4 judge 6.0 -> 3.33 on LLaMA3.2-1B; Math judge 8.33 -> 4.67). A downstream user finetuning or deploying the model in the watermark domain would suffer a clear quality penalty, which undermines the practicality argument; the 7.5% 'green' threshold appears arbitrary.

Guarantees are weaker than claimed. The Type-1 error control relies on the KGW null-hypothesis Z-test, which assumes watermarked and non-watermarked outputs are exchangeable/independent samples; after the adversary finetunes (potentially on in-domain data) or applies paraphrasing/scrubbing, the validity of the claimed FPR is not established. Only non-adversarial finetuning is systematically studied; the adversarial case (in-domain finetuning) degrades the signal substantially, and the Math domain cannot be recovered at all for Qwen.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only two base models (1B and 7B), only the KGW scheme, and only logit-distillation. No comparison to the other OSM watermarking families the paper itself discusses (weight perturbation [16, 19], classifier-based [18, 20]), and no adversarial attacks such as watermark scrubbing, paraphrasing, or output filtering that a suspicious deployer might use.

The stealthiness argument is largely qualitative and rests on a single anecdotal example (Fig. 5). No quantitative measure of detectability (e.g., classifier or human study distinguishing watermarked vs. non-watermarked in-domain outputs) is provided, despite stealthiness being a headline claim. Given the domain-restricted behavior, an adversary aware of fingerprinting via watermarks could plausibly detect or sanitize it.

Practicality caveats are underemphasized: reliable detection in the worst case requires up to 1,000 queries (Table 3, Fig. 3), and the method requires the provider to hold suitable, well-separated target-domain and regularization datasets; the domain-leakage analysis (App. C.3) shows specificity degrades sharply with even modest overlap, which the authors concede is hard to ensure for real-world domains.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: inconsistent model naming throughout (QWEN2.5-7B vs. QWEN2.5-3B), typos ('fingeprinting', 'they lacks robustness', 'id_fingerprinted', 'ressources/condicted'), and a summary table (Table 8) whose checkmarks rely partly on self-reported results from prior papers rather than a controlled comparison.

The overall narrative ('current OSM watermarks fail at fingerprinting; domain restriction fixes it') somewhat oversells an incremental fix; the significant residual weaknesses (in-domain quality loss, sensitivity to domain choice and leakage, in-domain finetuning vulnerability) are acknowledged only late in the paper.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing OSM watermarks fail at model provenance while backdoor-based fingerprints lack persistence, stealthiness, and robustness—and proposes a natural, relaxed alternative (domain-specific watermarking).

The technical framing is strong: the paper carefully articulates five desiderata (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness) and maps them to properties of watermarking (statistical Type-1 control, monotonicity), providing a principled justification rather than an ad-hoc method.

The method (Eq. 3 watermark distillation + Eq. 4 one-sided total-variation regularization) is simple, well-grounded, and the regularization loss has a clean interpretation (minimized iff distribution matches the teacher).

Comprehensive evaluation across reliability (Fig. 2), harmlessness (Tables 1-2: PPL, LLM-as-judge, and benchmarks), persistence under finetuning inside/outside the target domain (Table 3, Fig. 3), robustness to system prompts and greedy sampling (Fig. 4, 7, 8), and ablations on KGW hyperparameters (Fig. 9, Table 9).

Direct empirical comparisons with prior backdoor-based fingerprinting methods (instructional fingerprints [9], scalable fingerprints [15]) under identical finetuning and system-prompt protocols (Tables 4-7, Table 8) substantially strengthen the claims; prior methods degrade sharply under system prompts and finetuning while the proposed approach does not.

Useful additional analyses: watermark tokens as domain triggers, multiple co-existing keys, domain leakage sensitivity (Fig. 12), harmful-content domains, and an honest discussion of limitations (e.g., Math domain's low entropy, in-domain finetuning worst case).
Well-written, clear paper with a good balance of main-text results and supporting appendix; broader impact and resource/licensing details are addressed.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core technique is logit-distillation of an existing KGW watermark (Gu et al. [17]) restricted to a domain, plus a one-sided TV regularizer. The contribution is primarily a reframing/adaptation of known components rather than a fundamentally new method; domain restriction is a fairly natural mitigation once the failure modes of full OSM watermarking are known.

Scale of evaluation is limited: only two base models (Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-7B/3B, with an apparent naming inconsistency between the text ('Qwen2.5-7B') and figures/tables ('Qwen2.5-3B') that should be reconciled), and three domains. Larger models and more diverse domains would be needed to convincingly claim generality.

The adversarial analysis is incomplete: the paper mostly considers non-adversarial or naive finetuning. A knowledgeable adversary could (a) detect in-domain behavioral anomalies and finetune specifically on in-domain data (partially explored, worst case for Math cannot be recovered even with 1000 queries), or (b) apply watermark-removal/distillation attacks known from the watermarking literature. The threat model is stated but not fully stress-tested.

In-domain finetuning significantly degrades the signal (Table 3), and the recovery relies entirely on increasing query count (monotonicity). This means the method's persistence claim is conditional on the adversary's data and the provider's query budget; the Math failure case in App. A.1 shows this is not always recoverable.

Domain leakage analysis (App. C.3) reveals a real practical weakness: real-world domain separation between target and regularization data is difficult, and specificity degrades with as little as 10% leakage—this limits deployment realism for broad domains.

The paper assumes the provider can query the API in the target domain with substantial volume (up to 1000 queries); costs and API rate-limiting considerations are only briefly touched on ('under $1'), and stealthiness of many systematic in-domain queries from a single client is not analyzed.

Several minor writing issues (typos such as 'fingeprinting', 'id_fingerprinted', inconsistencies in model naming, Table 9 quality trade-off showing notably degraded judge scores/PPL in the target domain, e.g., PPL 11.1 vs 4.38 base), which slightly undercut polish.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new paradigm for black-box LLM fingerprinting: replacing brittle, memorized query-key pairs with a semantic query domain (e.g., French) and a statistical watermark signal. This reframing is well-motivated by a clear analysis of why query-key fingerprints fail (Sec. 3.1), and is technically sound.

The method is well-instantiated: in-domain watermark distillation (Eq. 1) combined with a novel one-sided total variation regularization loss (Eq. 2) that preserves the out-of-domain distribution. The ablation in App. C.4 convincingly shows the regularization loss matters for utility and stealth.

The evaluation is extensive and thorough: 3 models (1B, 3B, 8B), 25+ deployment scenarios (sampling, system prompts, quantization, pruning, finetuning, active adversaries) plus 5 targeted adversarial scenarios, with strong baselines (IF, SF) reproduced and fairly adapted to the instruction-tuning setting. The FSR metric is simple and interpretable.

The core robustness mechanism — detectability monotonically increasing with the number of queries (Figs. 3, 5) — is both demonstrated empirically (e.g., robustness against the anti-watermark paraphraser of Diaa et al. after ~50-100 queries) and grounded in theory: Theorem D.1 provides an asymptotic normality result with a variance correction term, giving principled FPR control for the concatenated-response detector.

Useful extensions beyond the main method: watermark trigger tokens with opening/closing tokens, multi-key conditioning (App. E.2), watermarking of the harmful domain for traceability (App. E.3), and multi-domain ablations (French/Math/Medicine). These enrich the contribution.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, compute budget, licenses of all datasets/models, and code included with the submission. Ethics and limitations are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The core technical machinery is largely assembled from prior work (Red-Green watermark, watermark distillation from Gu et al. 2024); the novelty lies mainly in the semantic conditioning and the regularization loss rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The individual components are predictable combinations, though the instantiation and empirical findings (e.g., conditioned watermarks being MORE robust to finetuning than full watermarks, App. B.3) are non-obvious and valuable.

The stealth evaluation (Sec. 5.3) relies on a single generic GPT5-MINI judge rather than adaptive, well-resourced adversaries. Prior work (Gloaguen et al. 2025a) shows watermarked models can be detected with targeted prompting; the stealth claim is only partially validated and partially argued, not tested.

Quality within the semantic domain is degraded more than the abstract implies: Table 4 shows the LLM-as-a-judge score on French drops substantially for LLAMA3.2-1B (5.10 to 3.18) and visibly for the other models. The paper acknowledges this and attributes it to watermark strength, but the trade-off analysis is mostly deferred to ablations.

The method requires the model owner to fix and later query a semantic domain with ~1000 queries, and the stealth advantage partially depends on the adversary not knowing the domain. A determined adversary who discovers the domain (e.g., by probing) could block all in-domain queries — a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not quantify (e.g., cost of such blocking vs. cost of legitimate French traffic).

Evaluation is limited to small/medium models (1B-8B) and the distillation setup may scale differently to larger models; only one watermarking scheme (Red-Green) is instantiated, and the FSR measurement (5 independent trials, binary averaging) provides limited statistical resolution at the tails.

strengths: The paper identifies real, well-motivated weaknesses of existing query-key fingerprinting (brittleness to deployment modifications and detectability of atypical keys) and proposes a coherent new paradigm: semantic domains as queries and statistical watermark signals as keys.

The instantiation is technically sound: it builds on watermark distillation (Gu et al., 2024) with a sensible regularizer (Eq. 2) that preserves the out-of-domain distribution, and the detection procedure inherits statistical guarantees, which the authors formalize via a corrected Z-test (Theorem D.1 with Lindeberg CLT proof).

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: 3 models, 8 benchmarks for utility, 25 deployment scenarios (sampling, system prompts, quantization, pruning, finetuning) plus 5 targeted adversaries, alongside ablations on number of queries, watermark strength, semantic domain, and regularization, and an extended study of semantically conditioned watermarks (trigger tokens, multiple keys, harmful domain).

The comparison against two prior baselines (IF, SF) is systematic, with a clearly defined Fingerprint Success Rate metric, and results support the central claim that only the proposed fingerprint remains detectable across all tested scenarios.
Reproducibility is addressed well: hyperparameters are detailed, code is included, and resource usage is reported.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core technique is a combination of existing components (Red-Green watermarking, watermark distillation) with a conditioning mechanism; the theoretical contribution is largely a variance-correction refinement of an existing detector rather than new methodology.

The stealth argument has a significant acknowledged hole: if the adversary learns the semantic domain (e.g., French), they can block or translate all domain queries, defeating the fingerprint. The paper's mitigation (high cost for the adversary) is asserted rather than quantified.

The choice of a semantic domain requires distorting the model's distribution on that domain. Table 4 shows a notable drop in LLM-as-a-judge scores on French (e.g., 5.10 to 3.18 for Llama3.2-1B), which contradicts the 'low impact on utility' narrative and could itself raise suspicion from users of that domain; this trade-off is only briefly discussed.
Experiments are limited to small models (1B-3B-8B); scalability to larger frontier models, where the fingerprinting scenario is most relevant, is untested.

The stealth evaluation relies on a single generic GPT5-MINI judge; the conclusion that outputs are stealthy would be more convincing with multiple detectors, including targeted watermark-detection attacks from the cited literature (Gloaguen et al., 2025a), rather than only discussing them.
Table 1 shows some utility drops that are not fully explained (e.g., HumanEval for Llama3.2-1B drops from 0.44 to 0.28), which weakens the 'negligible impact' claim on coding tasks.
The method only applies to models fingerprinted before release by the owner, restricting its applicability relative to the framing of the ownership-verification problem.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated paradigm shift: replacing brittle fixed query-key pairs with (i) broad semantic domains as queries and (ii) statistical watermark signals as keys. This reframing is intuitive, well-argued, and addresses real limitations of prior black-box fingerprinting methods.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: three instruction-tuned models (LLaMA3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-3B, LLaMA3.1-8B), 25 deployment scenarios (sampling, system prompts, quantization, pruning, finetuning) plus 5 targeted adversarial ones, with two strong baselines (IF, SF) and a clean, well-defined metric (FSR). Only their method achieves FSR 1.0 across all scenarios.

Technically sound instantiation: watermark distillation with a well-designed regularization loss (Eq. 2, one-sided total variation) that preserves out-of-domain distribution, supported by an ablation (App. C.4) and additional quality metrics (PPL, LLM-as-judge). Theorem D.1 provides a principled asymptotic analysis of the detector's FPR control, including a correction term missing from the original Kirchenbauer et al. test.

Good use of statistical signal properties: detectability increases monotonically with the number of queries (App. C.1, Figs. 3 and 5), which elegantly explains robustness even under targeted attacks (semantic-domain finetuning, adversarial paraphrasing) and gives the owner a tunable detection-cost knob.

Interesting and useful ablations: domain-entropy dependence of detectability (Fig. 6), watermark strength trade-off (Fig. 7), full-watermark vs. semantically-conditioned watermark robustness (Fig. 4), and extension to token-triggered watermarks, multiple keys, and harmful-domain watermarking (App. E) demonstrate breadth beyond the headline method.

Stealth is evaluated, not just claimed: the FPR/recall analysis with an LLM judge (Fig. 2) shows prior atypical query-key methods are easily detectable while theirs is not, and the paper is candid about when stealth fails (adversary knowing the domain).
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, resource description, licenses of all datasets/models, and code included with submission.
weaknesses: The stealth evaluation relies on a single GPT-5-MINI judge with prompts designed by the authors; a motivated malicious deployer with watermark-specific detection tools (e.g., Gloaguen et al., 2025a) or better statistical tests is only partially addressed. The adversarial threat model for stealth is weaker than for robustness.

The core stealth claim depends on the adversary not knowing the semantic domain. Once the paradigm is published, the search space of plausible domains (languages, math, medicine, code, etc.) is small and enumerable; the paper acknowledges this but the mitigation (cost of blocking) is speculative and not empirically evaluated.

Quality degradation is not fully negligible on the semantic domain: LLM-as-judge scores drop substantially on French text (e.g., 5.10 → 3.18 for LLaMA3.2-1B; 6.90 → 4.82 for LLaMA3.1-8B in Table 4), meaning users interacting in the domain may perceive a quality loss. This is downplayed relative to the benchmark results.

Only two baselines are compared, and both were originally designed for the completion setting and adapted to instruction-tuning by the authors; results for the baselines could be sensitive to these adaptations.

Detection requires concatenating replies from up to 1000 queries, which is fine for a hypothetical API setting but assumes the owner can obtain sufficient query volume and that the responses correspond to the semantic domain; scaling/cost considerations under rate-limiting or paid APIs are not discussed in depth.

The FSR measurement (5 independent detection runs) is thin for headline '100% detection' claims; confidence intervals are absent, and the sharp binary thresholding makes small-sample effects invisible.

Some 'first' claims (first semantically conditioned watermark, first stealthy-and-robust fingerprint) are strong relative to the breadth of related work surveyed; related methods combining backdoors with natural triggers are not deeply compared.
